As the government stalls on a response to key recommendations in the robodebt royal commission, it has legislated a huge expansion in the use of automated decision-making.

Legislation before parliament to reform the National Disability Insurance Scheme sets out an unprecedented expansion of automated government decision-making in reviewing support offered by the scheme. For what is believed to be the first time, it permits the automation of discretionary decisions rather than simply administrative calculations.

The bill explicitly allows for automation in cases where there is “(a) a discretion being exercised; (b) an evaluative judgement being made; (c) a state of mind being formed”.

“We haven’t come across this before,” says Ed Santow, a former Human Rights Commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute. “Generally, the advice that oversight bodies give to government is that discretion is something that is quintessentially a human task, and so automation should be more of those other sorts of non-evaluative judgements or calculations … Whereas discretion is something where a human is expected to exercise judgement.”

Santow says the power being proposed to automate decisions in the NDIS reform bill is incredibly broad. “Basically, it says that the government is able to decide which decisions are to be automated,” he says, “and those decisions may involve just that kind of calculation type question, as black and white questions, or they may involve discretion, or they may involve some combination of both.”

Santow, alongside colleagues Clare Brennan and Sarah Sacher, has raised these automation issues in a submission to the Senate inquiry into the NDIS reform bill. The inquiry has received more than 4000 submissions and hearings are set for the week ahead.

Santow says he has “grave” concerns about the legislation, which both allows for expansive use of automation and is scarce on safeguards.

“What this bill does is it creates what’s known as a facilitative power,” Santow says.

“It’s saying you can do this thing, you can kind of enable these automated decisions to take place. What we would also expect, and what’s not in the bill … are the safeguards that will make it much less likely that something will go wrong, and if something does go wrong, that the individual will be okay.”

According to the Australian Council of Social Service, the bill as it is currently drafted should not pass.

“Automation should not extend to discretionary decision-making,” says Jacqueline Phillips, the council’s executive director of policy and research. “These are extraordinary reforms in their scope and potential impact.”

Phillips says there should be human oversight in any decision where a person’s entitlements are reduced. “What’s quite extraordinary about the NDIS bill is it proposes very broad powers for the minister to delegate major areas of decision to automation but including discretionary decisions,” she says.

Labor is losing political skin on these reforms and associated savings measures, even as sustainability concerns about the scheme are widely shared. Over the next 10 years, a total of $184.9 billion will be taken out of the scheme, as its annual growth is restrained from more than 10 per cent to “5 to 6 per cent, or lower”. It is expected that 160,000 participants will be removed from the scheme.

The NDIS reforms are now at the forefront of growing concern about the expansion of automated decisions in government, as well as expansion in the use of artificial intelligence.

Twenty-three government agencies, from Services Australia and the Australian Tax Office to the Clean Energy Regulator and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, are authorised to use automated decision-making in their operations. A desktop review by the Australian Information Commissioner in January found only 17 per cent of the agencies disclosed that they used automated decision-making in their Information Publication Scheme, which they are required to do under the Freedom of Information Act.

The Commonwealth Ombudsman is investigating incorrect assessments under the aged home care Integrated Assessment Tool and there is a partial pause to the Targeted Compliance Framework for jobseekers receiving income support payments.

Officials from the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations indicated in Senate estimates this week that somewhere between 100,000 and more than 310,000 people have been affected by unlawful cancellation of social security payments, as brought to light by Economic Justice Australia.

There is a human override in the NDIS bill, but it is not expected to be widely used.

“It’s an unusual one,” Santow says. “The CEO of the NDIA [National Disability Insurance Agency] can override, but it’s a bit like the power that the immigration minister or home affairs minister exercises in our immigration and visa system, so it’s not like an internal review process, which would be a much more conventional thing.”

Adding to the anxiety within the disability community about cuts to participation is the lack of clarity and open-ended nature about where the automated discretion would apply, apart from the current trial of the I-CAN tool, an instrument designed to give holistic assessments of a person’s needs.

“Once AI starts coming into the way government’s running its services, that will explode, and we need to get the basics right now …”

“Our understanding is it could be applied overall,” says Megan Spindler-Smith, the acting chief executive of People With Disability Australia. “We currently have really deep concerns around the current I-CAN tool, because it’s only being tested on participants with non-complex or non-changing support needs. We don’t actually know if the decision-making that comes out of that, outside of non-complex spaces, is reasonable and actually meets the needs of the person with disability that it’s making decisions for.

“Other than the I-CAN tool, to the best of our understanding, and I’m saying to the best of our understanding, these systems have not been developed yet.”

The disability community wants to protect review rights. Currently disputed cases have access to the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART), but there is a request for clarity around automated decision-making.

“We have no guarantees that it is going to be an accessible process,” Spindler-Smith says. “If you are building an automated decision-making process and system on decisions that are currently being made by the NDIS, when the majority of NDIS cases that go to the ART are actually found in favour of the participants and against the decisions that are made by the NDIA, that shows that the NDIA actually gets it wrong, and that is why the safeguards are so essential.”

A government spokesperson told The Saturday Paper the bill has appropriate safeguards and that the use of automation is transparent and accountable. They also said NDIS participants will still have the right to seek a merits review through the ART.

“This bill will enable the NDIA to utilise a computer program to take certain administrative actions on behalf of a human where it is safe and responsible to do so,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “This will mean that our public servants can focus on more of the sophisticated tasks that require genuine human interaction and people can be supported in a more timely and consistent way.

“What we’ve set up in this bill is really an enabling power and we will step through this very carefully with the community how this will happen in practice.”

This new approach to automation comes as the Albanese government continues to deal with the fallout of the illegal robodebt scheme.

Last week, the social services minister outlined the government’s approach when questioned by the independent member for Curtin, Kate Chaney, about the legacy work of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme.

“Our approach is that in every case there needs to be human oversight of any of the use of AI,” Tanya Plibersek told parliament. “We don’t just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs, as was the case under robodebt, which caused such great suffering for 430,000 Australians.”

While these issues with automated decision-making continue, there is also a major gap in the government’s response to the robodebt royal commission.

The Saturday Paper understands Attorney-General Michelle Rowland is still working on a consistent whole-of-government automated decision-making response to the royal commission, 16 months after a consultation period of eight roundtables and a small survey ended.

Some groups have complained that it has been 18 months since they were actively involved. There are four outstanding recommendations remaining from the royal commission, three of which require legislation.

“It certainly doesn’t look like it’s being approached with any sense of urgency at all,” Kate Chaney tells The Saturday Paper.

“We are seeing an increased use of automated decision-making in aged care, in NDIS, and the NDIS changes proposed will increase that again. Once AI starts coming into the way government’s running its services, that will explode, and we need to get the basics right now before there is that change in the future,” Chaney says.

It is argued the problems being experienced now across government are due to inconsistencies in how automated decision-making is applied and the absence of a clear set of guidelines for government departments.

“It’s stalled in the sense that it’s not complete yet,” Spindler-Smith says. “We still don’t have those clearer protections. We still don’t have an understanding from the learnings of the robodebt experience, especially around the needs for controls, including transparency, review rights and oversight.”

The recommendation that the government accepted to “consider opportunities” for a consistent legal pathway for automation is regarded as “ongoing”. The recommendation for establishing or expanding an existing body to monitor automated decision-making is also regarded as “ongoing”, although the government says it is ensuring there is appropriate oversight of automation and that it may consider an appropriate oversight body.

The Saturday Paper understands that after the public consultation period, the Attorney-General’s Department moved to consulting other Commonwealth agencies and other stakeholders.

“Responding to the Royal Commission with meaningful, durable reform is a priority for the government, particularly where it strengthens the integrity, lawfulness and transparency of Commonwealth decision making,” a spokesperson for Rowland said in a statement.

“The ADM (automated decision-making) framework will be designed to improve accuracy and consistency of administrative decisions, embed robust safeguards, including transparency obligations, and ensure that ADM is used lawfully, responsibly, and with appropriate human oversight. The ADM framework will also enable agencies to use ADM to lift productivity and deliver faster, more reliable services that are aligned with community expectations.”

The Albanese government’s whole approach to AI has been “under-resourced, too slow and too passive”, according to Chaney.

She says the potential benefits and harms are both enormous.  “I’m concerned that there’s another robodebt in the making somewhere in the system,” she says. “We have to be really careful that we’re not losing the human out of our human services.

“And automated decision-making can help with the efficiency of decisions – it can reduce the cost of delivering government services – but only if there’s really clear understanding of how it’s being used, and that a human can actually override those decisions if necessary. Because humans have common sense, and we need to actually make sure that we’re not losing the humanity when we’re trying to look after people.”

In addition to these concerns, there are ongoing issues with the Targeted Compliance Framework operated by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, the automated regulatory and tracking system that unlawfully cancelled welfare payments between April 2022 and July 2024. It has been paused, but is due to come back online after a revamp in 2027.

“We’ve just received legal advice, which has confirmed EJA [Economic Justice Australia] concerns, where people are getting their payments suspended automatically because they’re not meeting a mutual obligation requirement,” says Kate Allingham, the chief executive of EJA. “Under the legislation, there is a requirement of discretion and we have concerns that an automated process is not adequately applying that discretion in the way that it should do lawfully.”

Economic Justice Australia, the peak body for community legal centres, previously found the government unlawfully cancelled more than 300,000 welfare payments. It spotted a coding error in an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and applied it to the number of people it would have affected and came up with 310,000.

“It is unlawful because there were timeframes in regard to the amount of time they had to respond, and that timeframe was reduced because of the coding error, and so there was less time for them to respond, and so the timeframes are within the legislation, and that is of really significant concern,” Allingham says. “It’s pretty easy to figure out that if there is a coding error that’s impacted one person, it could potentially be impacting thousands more.”

When Greens Senator Barbara Pocock questioned the 310,000 figure at Senate estimates on Wednesday, a department official said the number of unlawful cancellations was in the “vicinity of that”.

There was, the official said, complexity because there were people who had found employment and did not need to “reconnect” to the system under mutual obligations, so it may be a “much smaller cohort”.

The Anti-Poverty Centre estimated the figure for unlawful cancellations would then sit around 100,000, which is about 10 times the number the department previously admitted to.

Also causing concern in estimates this week was an aged-care tool brought in last November, in part to speed up long waiting lists for assessments for home care. The algorithm has been criticised for repeatedly under-assessing levels of need.

Departmental officials conceded that the department had not consulted before removing the ability for human assessors to override incorrect outcomes.

Under the current settings for the automated Integrated Assessment Tool, humans collect clinical data that is entered into the tool where universal aged-care rules apply. A second human assessor can review the data, but they can’t override the decision.

“The rules have to apply to everybody equally,” Minister for Aged Care and Seniors Sam Rae told the ABC on Thursday. “There’s a component. There’s a mathematical component that’s the nature of a process. An algorithm is just a process. There is a process by which the aged-care rules are applied, that’s an automated process.

“After the decision … the person can seek a review of the decision and that then comes back into a separate process. Another human being, a third human being, is part of the review process.”

Despite that defence, the minister has requested the department conduct a rapid three-month review of the “prioritisations mechanism” of the tool.

The Commonwealth Ombudsman is already investigating.

Karen Barlow is The Saturday Paper’s chief political correspondent.
